source.title: Aligning Agents like Large Language Models
source.authors: Adam Jelley; Yuhan Cao; David Bignell; A. Storkey; Sam Devlin; Tabish Rashid

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses whether LLM training ideas may transfer to decision-making agents and cites language-model scaling laws, but it does not test the stated language-model loss laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a visual-agent model-size comparison, not held-out language-model cross-entropy, power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its cited language-model scaling results are not its own results. The model-size comparison is recorded as a related finding about agents under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: Position paper with a proof-of-concept agent pipeline in a 3D game. It cites Kaplan/Hoffmann scaling laws but reports no loss-vs-scale power law, extrapolation, allocation, shape ablation or downstream-predictability fit. Its only scale result compares online task failure rates for three from-scratch agents (4M, 25M, 103M) trained on 300 trajectories, shown in a figure without fits. This is a related construct (task success of imitation agents), not the claim's loss law. It is recorded under fits_no_version. The reward-model accuracy vs comparisons trend ("approximately logarithmically") is also not a pretraining loss power law.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue agents should be trained with the LLM pipeline (pre-training, SFT, RLHF) and list scaling laws among ideas that may transfer. Their preliminary appendix finds larger agents fail less on the task, which they say agrees with Pearce et al. (2024). This does not establish any loss scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The size comparison measures online task success of visual imitation agents trained from scratch on task-specific data, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy across parameters, tokens, or compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Three agents (4M, 25M, 103M parameters) were trained from scratch on 300 task trajectories with the same number of updates. Task failure fell as parameter count increased; the 103M agent failed about 20% of the time. There were early, high-variance indications that larger models align faster under RL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For pixel-based imitation-learning agents, larger parameter count lowers online task failure at fixed small data.

fits_no_version.finding: Reward model test accuracy rises approximately logarithmically with the number of preference comparisons when the agent encoder is used (about 90% at 100 comparisons).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference reward-model accuracy for agents scales log-linearly with comparison count.

record.problems: The relevant model-scaling result is a preliminary agent experiment on one task-specific dataset and is shown in a figure without tabulated values or stated uncertainty. It does not measure the claim's language-model loss outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on the specified language-model claim were left out. Other reported outcomes concern agent alignment and reward-model performance rather than the versions tested here.

untested.parts: No held-out loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
Model sizes differ in depth and width together. There is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Agent scaling is shown only as three task-success points with no power-law form. Pearce et al. 2024 is cited, not tested.
No analysis of fitting choices or curve bending.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's rows carry state 'observed' with no linked version; these are changed to cannot_determine/none. No verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of larger language-model runs.
No controlled comparison of language-model architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The agent experiments do not measure whether the same power-law loss form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task predictability test for language models or relation between language-model pretraining loss and downstream performance.
No analysis of language-model exponent or allocation sensitivity to fitting choices, nor evidence of language-model loss curves bending.

relation.reason: Scaling laws are discussed as background and a potential transfer from LLMs to agents; no claimed scaling law is tested or used as a tool.

tranche.reason: The preliminary size comparison reports online task outcomes without testing power-law form, extrapolation, compute allocation, architecture invariance, downstream predictability, or fit dependence.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated 28 December 2025, although the pack lists 2024. Figure 12 supports a qualitative decrease in failure with size, without establishing a scaling law.
